feedback: 'Warm and cool sit in between hot and cold — that's why we can line things up from coldest to hottest.'
If a child uses only 'hot' and 'cold': 'Is it exactly hot, or more like warm? There are steps in between.'
For the freezer-to-bath strip: 'Nice ordering — the freezer is coldest and the warm bath hottest, with steps in between.'
activities.intendedInsight: The word 'temperature' names a sensation children already know, and warm and cool are the in-between points between hot and cold — it is a continuum, not two boxes.
learnerActions: Hold or look at things that are clearly warm, cool or cold (a warm drink, an ice cube, a sunny spot, cool shade) and say how each feels.
Match felt-experience cards — ice cube, warm drink, cool shade, hot sand — to the words hot, warm, cool, cold.
Order familiar places as a scale: freezer → fridge → room → warm bath, from coldest to hottest.
Decide for the air outside today whether it feels hot, warm, cool, or cold.
activities.title: Feel first, then name it

feedback: 'Warmer than yesterday — and you noticed the thermometer is higher today. Nice link.'
If the child only says 'hot': 'Compared with yesterday, is it warmer, cooler, or about the same?'
activities.intendedInsight: Comparative temperature language (warmer/cooler/about the same) describes how one day differs from another, tying the instrument to lived weather.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'Is it warmer or cooler than yesterday, and how do you know?'
Give the comparison in words and the reason (how it feels, or what the thermometer shows).
Connect the thermometer reading to the daily weather routine — check today against yesterday.
activities.title: Warmer or cooler than yesterday? Talk it through

feedback: When both read the same: 'They match — both sat in the same room, so both are at room temperature. The metal only FEELS colder.'

If a child predicted the metal is really colder: 'It feels colder because it pulls heat from your hand quickly — let's look at the thermometer: if both read about the same, they really are the same temperature.'
Fridge follow-up: 'Now the metal really is colder — because of where it has been, not because it's metal. Temperature depends on surroundings.'
Keep the conductivity point light at this age: name that metal feels colder without insisting 'metal is always colder.'
activities.intendedInsight: How something feels is not a reliable measure of its temperature: things that have sat together in the same room for long enough, away from sun and heaters, end up at about the same temperature even if the metal feels colder, because metal draws heat from your hand faster. A thermometer measures the object or air, not your sensation.
learnerActions: Leave a metal object and a wooden or plastic object side by side in the same room for at least an hour, away from sunlight, heaters and draughts.
Feel both, then predict what a thermometer will read on each — and say your reason BEFORE measuring.

With an adult, measure both by holding the same contact thermometer probe firmly against each object until the reading stops changing (do not use an infrared thermometer on shiny metal, which can read wrongly low), then compare the readings with your prediction.
Discuss: 'If both sat in the same room all morning, could they really be different temperatures?' and 'Which do you trust more to tell you the temperature — your hand or the thermometer?'
Try the follow-up: put the metal object in the fridge and leave the wooden one out, then measure both and say what changed.
activities.title: Same room, same temperature: feel versus measurement
